defect.title: Reopen from Dock or open -a does not restore the Status window
defect.note: applicationShouldHandleReopen calls makeKeyAndOrderFront when hasVisibleWindows is false. After AX close: glass_probe axWindowCount=0, extras still present. proctor_apps activate: activated true, windows [], 8000ms, note says menu-bar-only. open -a /Applications/Proctor.app: still axWindows=0. System Events click Window/Proctor restored 640x592 at 946,99. Likely cause: after walkthroughCompleted=1 the app is .accessory and NSApp.windows.first is not ordered front by activate/open -a; the Window menu item is. Fixed: WindowPresentation.shouldPresentMain asks whether a window titled Proctor is on screen instead of trusting hasVisibleWindows; reopen orders it front or posts for the scene to be created. Verified on .build/Proctor.app: cg 0 / ax 0 before, cg 1 820x1009 / ax 1 after open -a. Six tests in WindowPresentationTests cover the rule. Verified on the installed artifact after reinstall: cg 0 / ax 0 before, cg 1 640x592 / ax 1 titled Proctor after open -a.

defect.title: Status window kept claiming Ready while the agent was wedged
defect.note: First filed against a killed agent and retracted: a kill fails connect() at once and the window recovers within one 2s tick (Agent down at t+0.71s). Sweep L half-open found the real shape. With the agent held by SIGSTOP the socket is accepted and never answered, the poll blocks in read(), isChecking latches, and the window showed Ready with green grants past 25 seconds while a driven proctor_doctor never returned. Fixed by an opt-in SocketClient.ioTimeoutSeconds, default 0 so the shim is unchanged, with AgentModel polling at 5s. Verified: Agent down at t+7.12s, recovered after SIGCONT.

defect.title: Installed Proctor.app is Developer ID signed but not notarised or stapled
defect.note: spctl -a -vv /Applications/Proctor.app → rejected, source=Unnotarized Developer ID, origin=Developer ID Application: Luke Rhodes (H4HGFL52W7). stapler validate → does not have a ticket stapled. codesign reports runtime hardened, timestamp 18 Aug 2026. This is the artifact the macos-glass lane attached (commit 1c6500c51b24). CASE-0024 fails on it. Fixed by scripts/install.sh on 2026-08-19: notarised through the proctor keychain profile and stapled. spctl now returns accepted, source=Notarized Developer ID; stapler validate passes.

defect.title: Campaign recorded a refusal the product does not perform (profile filtering)
defect.note: CASE-0002 was armed with "swapped profile filter from full to core; verified proctor_guest refused". Measured: a core-profile shim executes proctor_guest and proctor_policy when they are named. That is the documented contract (MCPServer.swift:123) rather than a product defect, so the campaign record was corrected and the arming rewritten around what the profile does change, the advertised catalogue: 21 names on full, 10 on core.

defect.title: The drawn pointer was not excluded from screen capture
defect.note: Found while arming CASE-0008: with the exclusion at its default the run panel and the takeover tint reported sharingState 0 and refused every capture, while the drawn pointer reported 1 and photographed cleanly at 3456x2234. It covers every display, so Proctor's own pointer entered any display-scoped capture taken during a run, against the principle the other two panels are built on. Cause: it is the only one of the three that changes window level at runtime, and sharingType does not survive the change. Fixed by setting level and sharing together in one place. The obvious suspect, that the window server refuses .none at screenSaver level, was measured and ruled out first.

defect.title: Three commands declared for the menu bar were never rendered in it
defect.found: proctor_menu against the running app, compared with CommandSurface.all
defect.detail: Clear Waiting Runs, Takeover Notice and Drawn Pointer were declared with surfaces: [.menuBar] and SwiftUI never declared them. commandsMissingFromMenuBar could not see it: it compares the catalogue against its own surfaces field, so it passes whether or not a command renders. The published count was wrong too — 21 was the number of MCP tools, not commands; the catalogue holds 20.
defect.fix: The two drawing switches became toggles bound to the saved value. Clearing the queue needed a route: RunQueueControl is the queue's own vocabulary, kept disjoint from the run's because an existing test refuses a queue word in RunHUDControl, and proctor_queue is internal for the same reason proctor_hud is.

defect.title: The permissions list omitted the one permission whose absence is silent
defect.found: Photographing the status window and comparing it against the design of record
defect.detail: The design draws Input Monitoring; the window drew Automation and not it, because the health report never carried it. Grants.inputMonitoringState() already read it for the takeover path, and its own comment names the consequence: an operator who turned the input block on can find it silently unavailable. StatusSurface.ID.all named Input Monitoring and omitted Automation, so the uniqueness test was checking a set that did not describe the surface.
defect.fix: The health report carries Input Monitoring, never required. The identifier list names all five grants the report can carry.

defect.title: Three of the supervision TUI's five panes had no data source
defect.found: Driving proctor tui against a live wave-9 agent
defect.detail: Only run and queue were fed by the pushed frame. Readiness, switches and history drew their empty state whatever the machine was doing, and the empty state reads as a quiet machine rather than as a pane nobody wired.
defect.fix: Readiness and switches are filled from proctor_doctor. History is filled from proctor_history, which the first disposition wrongly recorded as unreachable. Two things were wrong with that reasoning. The verb exists: it is an internal socket verb the app's own History window already calls, kept out of ToolCatalogue so the shim, which gates tools/call on the catalogue, cannot route a model to it. And keeping it off the catalogue was never what made the trail unreadable to a model, because proctor_policy action audit is a catalogue tool that already opens the trail and hands back whole records. The projection this pane draws is strictly narrower than that one, so reading it here opens no path that was not already open and changes neither the sealing nor the gate. The pane also now separates a quiet machine from a trail this Mac could not open, and states the count of entries that could not be opened rather than drawing a history that is silently short. TUIHistoryPaneTests, 9 tests, armed.

defect.title: A halted caller was told which surface stopped it, and it was the wrong one
defect.found: Pressing s in proctor tui and reading the MCP caller's own result
defect.detail: The error said 'a person stopped this run from Proctor's run HUD'. Stop is reachable from the run panel, the menu bar and the TUI, and RunControl.shared is the same latch for all three, so a message naming one of them is wrong two times in three.
defect.fix: The message names the act rather than a surface.

defect.title: The permissions pane clipped its fourth row off the bottom
defect.found: The readiness pane against a live agent, after DEF-007 added a grant
defect.detail: The panel was drawn at a fixed nine rows against the three grants the design carried. A fourth grant was dropped silently, which is the one failure a permissions list must not have.
defect.fix: The panel is sized to the rows it is given, with the design's height as a floor.

defect.title: The fix reached the CLI and the TUI and was filtered out of the window
defect.found: Re-photographing the status window after DEF-007 and counting three rows where four were expected
defect.detail:
StatusChecks classifies every grant name the health report can carry, and an unrecognised name falls to .tool — deliberately, because tool names are the half that grows. Input Monitoring was unrecognised, so the window's permissions filter removed it while the CLI and the TUI, which do not filter, both drew it.

The net that exists for exactly this did not fire. The drift test scans SessionDoctor.swift for `.init(name: "` and asserts set equality against the map, and the new grant was written as `.init(` then a newline then `name:` — so the scan never saw the name, both sets lacked it equally, and the assertion passed. Its only guard was against finding NOTHING, and it found plenty.
defect.fix: Input Monitoring is classified as a live-read permission. The scan is a whitespace-tolerant regular expression with a count floor, because a partial scan passes set equality against a map that is short by the same names.

defect.title: The status window's chrome diverges from its design of record
defect.found: be-my-witness judging the capture against the design pane, both dark, both 640 wide
defect.detail:
Section headers are letter-spaced uppercase where the design specifies sentence case semibold and states the reason in its own caption: a header that recedes under what it labels. The build opens with a title block the design does not draw, grant rows use a tick glyph and a second line where the design uses a left icon and a right-hand pill, and Ready is a sentence inside the section rather than a pill on its header.

The header rule is fixed: SectionTitle drew letter-spaced monospaced capitals and now draws sentence case semibold in the secondary tier, which is the rule the design states and argues for. Re-captured and re-judged.
defect.fix: Three parts, and they were settled by two different means. The header rule the design argues for in its own caption was applied to the build: SectionTitle drew letter-spaced monospaced capitals and now draws sentence case semibold in the secondary tier. The title block and the Ready sentence were settled by a person choosing between them: keep the explanation, so the design of record was moved to carry both rather than the build stripped to match. Re-capturing to check that found a second fault — the build capture the earlier verdict rested on predated the rebuild of the header fix, so it showed the old treatment while the source drew the new one; re-taken from a process started after the rebuild. The design was also short a grant: it listed three where the build lists four, and Automation is now in it. One difference is left rather than closed and is recorded on the SURF-008 verdict: the design's grant row says what a grant is for and the build's does not, and closing it either way costs something nobody asked to spend.

defect.title: The walkthrough's first slide diverges from its design of record
defect.found: be-my-witness judging the capture against the design pane
defect.detail: The build leads with a three-segment progress bar and 'What Proctor does'; the design leads with a bordered icon and 'A model can test this Mac', and carries three capability chips the build replaces with two paragraphs and a callout.
defect.fix: Settled by the same decision. The build leads with a three-segment progress bar, 'What Proctor does', two paragraphs and a callout; the design led with an icon, 'A model can test this Mac' and three capability chips. Keep the explanation, so the design of record now carries the build's composition. Nothing was lost with the chips: they compressed what the first paragraph says in prose. SURF-009 re-judged and passes.

defect.title: The suite carried an assertion that could not fail, and five tests it was not counting
defect.found: scripts/campaign/cannotfail_swift.py, written because warrant:assay's two scanners read TypeScript, JavaScript and Python and this suite is Swift
defect.detail: Across 103 files and 1,653 @Test functions the scan returned seven findings. One was a real hole: BuildInfoTests asserted `captured.builtAt == captured.builtAt`, a stored property compared to itself, in the test whose whole claim is that the captured value does not move when the file underneath it is replaced. It would have passed on a build where builtAt re-read the path on every access, which is the regression it is named after. Three more asserted only by not throwing, so they passed just as happily with the guard they are about deleted. Two were the scan's own false positives on a house style that asserts through a same-file helper. A sixth pattern was added after those: a defaulted read. `(try? read()) ?? ""` binds an input that could not be read to an empty one, and an assertion about what is ABSENT from an empty value passes for the wrong reason. Two in the suite, both in the audit trail's own tests, and both making the claim the trail exists to support: one asserted a redacted address is nowhere in the file, the other that a rotation leaves no backup or sidecar. Each passed just as happily when there was no file and no directory listing to look in.
defect.fix: The tautology now pins the value before the replacement and compares against that; armed by standing in what a re-reading implementation would report, and it bites. The three implicit tests say `#expect(throws: Never.self)`. The evidence writer, which asserted nothing at all, now reads its artifact back. The scan follows a same-file helper one level, which removes the false positives. Arming the scan found a defect in the scan: a one-line test body balances its braces on the signature line, so the line-based body finder skipped it and then consumed the next function's body looking for an opening brace. Rewritten to match braces by character, which raised the denominator from 1,648 @Test functions to 1,653 — five tests it had never been counting. Re-armed with four seeded defects across both shapes, all four caught, and clean on the real suite at 0 of 1,653. The two defaulted reads now read with `try`, so an unreadable trail fails the test rather than satisfying it, and each states positively that the thing it is about is there before asserting what is not. The pattern is a finding only where the defaulted value feeds a negated assertion inside the same test body, because a positive assertion on an empty value still fails. A seventh pattern counts rather than fails: a bare return above the first assertion. Three in the suite, all documented as conditional on a toolchain being present. Whether their guards hold on this machine is a separate question from whether they are honestly written, and it was settled by inverting each assertion and watching all three go red, so none of them returned early here.

defect.title: The live Maestro lane could not run on this machine, and its two tests fought over one simulator
defect.found: Running the opt-in live lane, which had not been run since 15 Aug, against a real simulator and a real Maestro
defect.detail: Two faults, and the product was right about the first one. The lane passed `device: nil` and relied on exactly one simulator being booted. Four are booted here, so the product refused, named all four and asked for one — correctly — and the whole live lane went red for a fact about the machine rather than about the code, which is the failure its opt-in switch exists to prevent. The second only appears when both tests run. They drive one simulator, and run concurrently they interleave on it: the determinism check scored its two repeats as divergent at command 4, a real divergence caused by the sibling test tapping the device mid-repeat. Alone the repeat test passed in 27s; as a suite it failed after 317s. A resource shared by two tests is a test-order dependency wearing a green tick.
defect.fix: The lane reads PROCTOR_LIVE_MAESTRO_DEVICE, falls back to the single booted simulator when there is exactly one, and otherwise does not run — naming a device on the operator's behalf would drive a simulator they may be using. The suite is `.serialized`. Measured 20 Aug 2026 against maestro 2.4.0 and a booted iPhone 16 Pro on iOS 18.2: both tests pass, 55.6s for the suite, green twice.

defect.title: TUISurface.Model's equality could not tell two models apart, and nothing noticed
defect.found: scripts/campaign/mutate_swift.py, written because warrant:assay's generator reads .ts .tsx .js .jsx .mjs .cjs .py and this package is Swift
defect.detail: 24 mutants over TUISurface, CLISurface, StatusChecks and RunHUDMenuBar: 14 killed, 10 survived, 0 unbuildable — a 41.7% survival rate. The survivors were not scattered. Every one of the ten was in TUISurface.Model's hand-written `==`. Flipping any `&&` there to `||` makes two models that differ in one field compare equal; flipping any field's `==` to `!=` makes two identical models compare unequal. Neither was noticed by 1,666 tests. The operator has no caller in the product today, which is why it survived and also why it was worth pinning: the obvious optimisation for the render loop is to skip a redraw when the model has not changed, and an `==` that cannot tell two models apart turns that into a screen that stops updating while a run is moving, which is the one failure this surface exists to prevent. It is hand-written, so a field added to Model and forgotten in `==` compiles, ships and is invisible.
defect.fix: TUIModelEqualityTests pins it three ways: two models built the same way are equal, a difference in any one of the thirteen fields makes them unequal, and every stored property Mirror can see has a variant in the list — a floor rather than a mirror of the operator, because reflection cannot see which fields a hand-written `==` reads, so a new field fails on the count before anybody has to notice it is missing from the comparison too. Re-measured with the same seed and the same targets, so it is the identical 24 mutants: 24 killed, 0 survived. 41.7% survival to 0%.

defect.title: Eight of the CLI's twenty-one verbs could not be given their main argument
defect.found: Checking a parked assumption in spec-PRO-0073.md against the code, rather than by anything failing
defect.detail: The spec recorded the step-batch fork and the assumption taken to unblock it: "support both, stdin JSON as the documented path". Neither half was built. Every flag value was typed as a string, a number or a bool, so `--steps '[…]'` reached the agent as a string and came back `proctor_act requires steps as an array`; and nothing in the CLI read stdin at all. Eight verbs declare an array or an object argument — act, zoom, wait, assert, flow, stability, computer and policy — so 8 of 21 could not be called for the thing they exist to do. `proctor act` in particular could not actuate anything.
defect.fix: CLIArguments in Core, so the decision is asserted against values written by hand rather than only reachable through a live agent. A flag value opening with [ or { is parsed as JSON and left as its string when it does not parse, because a caller who typed a selector should not be told their selector is malformed JSON. Arguments on stdin are merged underneath the flags, so a flag beside a pipe retargets a recorded batch instead of silently doing nothing. The first version inferred the stdin read from isatty and hung: any caller whose stdin is an open pipe nothing writes to — a CI runner, an agent harness — is not a terminal either, and `proctor doctor` waited forever on a read that never returned. Found by running it. It is now an explicit `-` or `--stdin`, which is the conventional idiom, cannot hang, and is still stdin as the documented path. Verified against a live wave-9 agent on all four paths: a JSON flag reached the agent as an array and got the tool's own answer; a piped batch performed a real foregrounded actuation; a flag beside a pipe won; and malformed stdin printed what was wrong and the remedy. The remedy string and the parser's token are pinned to each other by a test, because the first draft printed a remedy for a flag that did not exist.

defect.title: Half of ProctorCore's sampled mutants survived, and the second hand-written equality was one of them
defect.found: Widening the mutation assay from 4 files to all 77 of ProctorCore
defect.detail: 1,991 mutation sites over 77 files. 60 were selected by a recorded seed and 49 ran before the run was killed; 48 scored, 24 killed and 24 survived, 1 unbuildable. **50% survival**, which is in the range the literature would predict and is the first honest number this suite has had for anything wider than four files. 13 of the 24 survivors are integer literals, many of them geometry and layout constants in pure values. 11 are logic, and three were read closely: `RunHUDSurface.Chip.==` compared field counts and nothing had ever compared two chips with different counts — the second hand-written Equatable this wave has found unwatched, after TUISurface.Model, and the same shape both times because Swift cannot synthesise `==` over an array of tuples. The other two are equivalent mutants rather than gaps. `RunHUDGate.onSegment`'s `<=` boundary is unreachable: `onSegment` is only called from `crosses`, `crosses` only when no point is `contains`, and `contains` uses `>=`/`<=` on both axes, so every point that could exercise the boundary was caught one step earlier. `RunHistory`'s `a.offset < b.offset` sort tiebreak differs from `<=` only for equal offsets, and offsets are unique enumeration indices.
defect.fix: RunHUDChipEqualityTests pins field count, field name, field value and order, plus the empty chip. Armed against the exact mutant that survived — `count ==` to `count !=` — and it now fails five assertions. The two equivalent mutants are recorded rather than chased: a survivor no test could kill is not a gap, and a suite contorted to kill one is worse than the survivor. The remaining survivors are a named backlog with a number against them rather than an absence: 24 of 48 scored, of which 13 are integer literals and 8 are logic sites not yet read.

defect.title: The operator CLI exits 0 when a check fails, and its test passes because it invents the reply shape
defect.found: Phase 5 of the full campaign: writing the first case the cli lane has ever had, and running the real binary against the live agent
defect.detail:
CLISurface.exit(forReply:lane:) decides the process exit code. Its assertion branch reads `$0["ok"]?.boolValue == false` on each element of `assertions`. The product never puts an `ok` key on an assertion element: SessionAssert.swift:45 writes `"status": .string(result.status.rawValue)`, one of pass/fail/skipped. `nil == false` is false, so the predicate matches nothing and the function returns .ok. Neither the top-level `"ok": .bool(failed == 0 && skipped == 0)` at SessionAssert.swift:81 nor the top-level `"failed"` count at :77 is consulted at all.

MEASURED, twice, against the live agent from .build/debug/proctor-cli:
  proctor assert --window win:4:0 --assertions '[{"kind":"exists","identifier":"a-control-that-does-not-exist-xyzzy"}]'
    reply: {"ok":false,"passed":0,"failed":1,"assertions":[{"status":"fail",...}]}   exit=0, expected 1
  proctor wait --window win:4:0 --condition nodeExists --identifier a-control-that-does-not-exist-xyzzy --timeoutMs 1200
    reply: {"ok":false,"timedOut":true,...}                                            exit=0, expected 1

A third instance is present by inspection and not yet measured: proctor_kill emits a top-level `"failed"` count at SessionKill.swift:73 which nothing reads.

This defeats the stated purpose of the surface. spec-PRO-0073.md's exit table says '1 means the call worked and your check failed' and '1 and 3 must never be confused: one is a failed check, the other is nothing measured'. A CI job running `proctor assert` reads 0 and concludes the assertion passed while the JSON on its stdout says it failed.

WHY NOTHING CAUGHT IT: Tests/ProctorCoreTests/CLISurfaceTests.swift:175 'a failed assertion exits 1 — the call worked and the check did not' builds its own reply, `.object(["assertions": .array([.object(["ok": .bool(true)]), .object(["ok": .bool(false)])])])`, which is a shape the product does not emit. The test asserts a value the test itself wrote, so it passes against a fiction while the real path exits 0. Same shape as the A7 finding the PRO-0076 verifier caught: an assertion standing on a value constructed by the test rather than produced by the code under test.
defect.fixedBy: Sources/ProctorCore/CLISurface.swift:148-155 reads the top-level ok, the top-level failed count, and each assertion status == "fail"

defect.title: proctor_capture reports a fully transparent frame as status complete and trustworthy true
defect.found: PRO-0078 phase 6, building the REQ-004 effect witness: the first capture was taken of a Proctor-owned window, and the picture was read rather than trusted
defect.detail:
proctor_capture on win:1:0, CG window 121564, a window Proctor's own UI process owns, returned {"status":"complete","trustworthy":true,"dirtyRectCount":1,"dirtyArea":0,"width":1520,"height":1936,"scale":2}. Every one of the 2,942,720 pixels in the resulting PNG is RGBA(0,0,0,0). Measured by decompressing the IDAT stream and counting: alpha histogram is {0: 2942720}, and no pixel has a non-zero byte in any channel.

The emptiness itself is almost certainly correct behaviour. Proctor excludes its own windows from its own captures so the HUD and the takeover statement do not appear in a shot, and an excluded window has nothing to deliver. The problem is that nothing in the reply says so. A caller asking for a picture of an excluded window gets `complete` and `trustworthy`, and dirtyArea 0 is the only hint, next to dirtyRectCount 1 which reads as though something changed.

Evidence: docs/test-campaign/evidence/witness/a1-capture.json and docs/test-campaign/evidence/witness/a1-agent-capture.png. The contrast is docs/test-campaign/evidence/witness/a1b-capture.json against Calculator, a window Proctor does not own, which returns a frame carrying the target's actual content.

NOT FIXED HERE. The fix is a design call about what proctor_capture should say when the target is one it excludes, and PRO-0078 is a witness item rather than a capture-semantics item. Recorded so it is visible.

WHY IT MATTERS TO THE CAMPAIGN: the effect-witness and raster-visual rungs both rest on a frame status, and this is a measured case of a status bit reading complete over a frame with no content in it. A raster case whose subject is an excluded window would pass every gate the campaign has.

defect.title: A run whose MCP peer dies keeps the agent queue past the 900-second pause backstop
defect.found: PRO-0078 phase 6, driving the glass lane: three separate runs stranded this way and each one had to be cleared by restarting the agent
defect.detail:
When the shim process driving a run exits while a run is in flight, the run stays in the agent's queue holding the slot. Every subsequent proctor_act returns queueBusy with 'another session was driving this Mac ... gave up without running any step', so the lane is unusable until the agent is restarted.

MEASURED: docs/test-campaign/evidence/witness/a4-stranded-run-queue.json reads heldForSeconds 552 with reason frontmostChanged; docs/test-campaign/evidence/witness/a4-stranded-run-queue-2.json reads the same run at 932 seconds, still held. The documented pause backstop is 900 seconds, so the second reading is past it and the run is still there.

Happened three times in one session, each time after the driving process died rather than after any product action. NOT FIXED HERE: the repair is in run lifecycle and belongs to whoever owns the queue, not to a witness item.

defect.title: Forty events swallowed by the takeover block produced no yield and no held reason
defect.found: PRO-0078 phase 6, building the REQ-007 effect witness across three runs
defect.detail:
The takeover block's tap calls onPersonInput for every event it declines to deliver, and SessionTakeover.swift:137 wires that to ContentionMonitor.noteUserInput, which sets the field ContentionWatch reads to decide the userInput condition.

MEASURED across three runs driven with a helper process posting into the session while the run held the foreground: the agent reported swallowing 6, 24 and 10 events (docs/test-campaign/evidence/witness/a45b-act.json, a4-act.json, a4c-burst.json). No run recorded a yield: yields is null in all three act results. Six consecutive proctor_doctor reads of the live queue during the third run report the active run with held reason null (docs/test-campaign/evidence/witness/a4-poll.json).

The path is not dead in general: a yield on a different reason was captured in the same session, at docs/test-campaign/evidence/witness/a4-stranded-run-queue.json, reason frontmostChanged.

This may be correct by design. PersonInput.isAPerson requires sourcePid == 0, so a helper's events are correctly not a person, and the swallow count rising without a yield may be exactly the intended asymmetry. What is not established either way is whether the userInput yield fires for a real hand on a real keyboard, because nothing in this session could post at pid 0. Recorded as the open half of CASE-0062.

defect.title: An agent window reports sharingState 1 where CASE-0032 records all three overlays at 0
defect.found: PRO-0078 phase 6, sampling the window server for the REQ-006 witness
defect.detail:
CASE-0032 records that all three Proctor overlays report sharingState 0 at the default, which is what keeps them out of other applications' captures. Sampling CGWindowListCopyWindowInfo from a separate probe process on agent pid 86732 found the run HUD panel (window 121489, layer 25) and the takeover statement (window 121490, layer 24) both at sharingState 0 as recorded, and alongside them window 121491 at layer 0, 1710x1073, reporting sharingState 1, present whether or not a run is in flight.

Evidence: docs/test-campaign/evidence/witness/a2-hud-11.json and a2-hud-12.json.

Whether window 121491 is one of the three CASE-0032 means is not established here. It may be an ordinary agent window that the claim was never about. Recorded because a reader comparing the two would otherwise have to work that out from scratch. NOT FIXED HERE.

defect.title: A bounded-probe test asserts wall-clock elapsed and fails on a loaded machine
defect.found: PRO-0078 phase 6: three consecutive ./scripts/test.sh runs while the glass lane agent was live
defect.detail:
Tests/ProctorAgentTests/ScreenRecordingProbeWiringTests.swift:42, in 'a platform call that never answers returns unconfirmed within the bound', asserts `elapsed < 5.0` around a probe whose bound is 0.2 seconds. The comment calls the 25x headroom generous so it does not flake on a loaded machine.

MEASURED: with a signed Proctor agent live on the glass lane and captures in flight, the same test recorded elapsed 5.016569018363953 on one run and 10.252003073692322 on the next, failing the whole suite both times: 'FAIL: swift test exited 1 ... 1814 tests in 214 suites failed'. With the agent stopped and nothing else running, the same command passed: 'PASS: Test run with 1814 tests in 214 suites passed after 21.366 seconds'.

The behaviour under test is correct in all three runs; the probe returned .unconfirmed every time. What moved was the wall clock. A 25x margin on a 0.2 second bound is 4.8 seconds of scheduler slack, and this machine consumed all of it and then twice that.

NOT FIXED HERE, and deliberately not: a gate edited to make it green is a finish line that moved, and the choice between a larger margin, a mocked clock and a relative assertion belongs to whoever owns the probe. Recorded because a suite that fails under load fails in CI, where load is the normal condition.

defect.title: REQ-024's declared effect class and provider name a boundary the browser-routing path never crosses
defect.found: PRO-0083 W8: building the effect witness the census asked for, and finding nothing to witness
defect.detail:
inventory.json records REQ-024 ("Automatic browser routing dispatches web URLs to Obscura or browser-use engines") with effect `subprocess` and provider "Process() in Sources/ProctorAgent/Actuation/CuaClients.swift — obscura and cua-driver". Neither is on the browser-routing path, established in source rather than asserted:

- `BrowserTarget` is pure by its own header: "The agent supplies what it read from the accessibility tree as a WebContentProbe; this file decides."
- `Session.browserHandoff` returns a disclosure that `SessionAct` and five other call sites attach to a reply. Nothing executes.
- `ToolProbe`'s header reads "Whether Obscura is on this machine, cached, and never executed", and `ToolLocator.locate` decides availability with `isExecutable(path)` — a stat, not a spawn.
- `grep -rn 'Process()' Sources/` returns eleven sites across eight files: the guest providers, simctl, the cua driver, `shortcuts run`, the dictionary, the installer and the UI. Not one is reached by a browser handoff.

The two `Process()` sites in CuaClients.swift are real and do spawn `cua-driver`, but they belong to the CUA delegation lane, not to browser routing. The only boundary the browser capability crosses is a filesystem READ, and the campaign's closed effect-class list (subprocess, outbound-socket, inbound-socket, packet-filter, multicast, filesystem-write, device, ipc, none) has no member for it — `filesystem-write` is its only filesystem class.

CONSEQUENCE: `campaign.py check` will demand a `subprocess` witness for REQ-024 forever, and the only way to make it green is to fabricate one or to reclass the requirement to `none`. Both are finish lines that moved. CASE-0087 therefore resolves `inconclusive` with the instrument named, and measures the read that does happen: the production `ToolLocator.locate` over two real directories, answering `missingCompanions [obscura-worker]` for one and none for the other, with `chmod 0600` taking availability to false.

NOT FIXED HERE, and deliberately. Rewriting REQ-024's row would be this item editing the registry it is being measured against. The fix is either a `filesystem-read` class in the campaign's vocabulary or a corrected provider field, and both belong to whoever owns the census.

defect.title: campaign.py check prints a capped list of unwitnessed requirements, and the cap reads as the population

`campaign.py check` prints at most twelve requirements under "External-effect claims with no witness", and at most twenty per pass elsewhere. Nothing in the output says the list is truncated, and no denominator is printed beside it.

MEASURED: the external set is 22 requirements — `len([r for r in inventory['requirement'] if r.get('effect') not in (None, 'none')])`. NOT FIXED HERE: `campaign.py` is the skill's tool and lives outside this repo (~/.claude/plugins/cache/fledgeling-plugins/test-campaign/0.9.2/). defect.title: PolicyStore has no test seam, so a test that configures the policy writes the operator's real policy file
defect.found: PRO-0083 W2: a witness drove `proctor-cli policy --action configure --block` against its own in-process server
defect.detail:
`AuditLog` carries `seams.directory` and an `isTestProcess` interlock precisely so a test cannot write the operator's trail. `PolicyStore` carries neither. `PolicyStore.directory` is computed straight from `homeDirectoryForCurrentUser`, and `Session.configurePolicy` calls `PolicyStore.save(policy)` unconditionally.

MEASURED 2026-08-21: PRO-0083's REQ-034 witness drove `policy --action configure --block ["com.fledgeling.witness"]` through a real `proctor-cli` child against a private test socket. That created ~/Library/Application Support/app.fledgeling.procter/policy/policy.json on this machine — the operator's own file, not a redirected one — with the test's bundle id on the block list. The file's birth time was the minute the run started, so nothing of the operator's was overwritten on this occasion; `configurePolicy` replaces the whole block set, so on a machine where one had been configured it would have been.

The blast radius is not limited to the writing test. PRO-0077's REQ-015 witness drives an audited run against `com.fledgeling.witness`, and it then failed with `policyDenied: com.fledgeling.witness is on the block list; actuation is refused` in a LATER run in which PRO-0083's suites were skipped entirely — the block had outlived the process that wrote it. A test that fails because of a file another test left on disk yesterday is the kind of flake that gets a real finding dismissed.

REPAIRED, NOT FIXED. The leaked entry was removed from the operator's file and the witness no longer drives `configure` at all; CASE-0081 records that the policy gate is therefore unreachable from that lane and says so rather than dropping it silently. The fix is a `seams.directory` on `PolicyStore` matching `AuditLog`'s, which is a production change and belongs to whoever owns the policy rail.

defect.title: Session.doctor blocks a cooperative thread inside SecStaticCodeCheckValidity, and fourteen such tests saturate the pool
defect.found: PRO-0083: the full suite stopped returning a verdict once nine integration tests were added beside it
defect.detail:
`Session.doctor` reaches `SignatureVerdictCache.verdict(for:)` for the cua-driver, which calls `CuaPreflight.verifySignature` and blocks in `SecStaticCodeCheckValidity` -> `Security::Dispatch::Group::wait()`. It is a synchronous blocking call made from inside the session actor, so it occupies a Swift cooperative-pool thread for its whole duration, and that pool has exactly `activeProcessorCount` threads and never grows.

MEASURED 2026-08-21, by `sample` on the wedged process, repeatedly: fourteen to fifteen of the sixteen cooperative threads inside that one call, in `BrowserLaneWiringTests`, `ObscuraPresenceWiringTests`, `ScreenRecordingProbeWiringTests`, `GuestDoctorWiringTests`, `MachineDisclosureWiringTests`, `DoctorReplyWiringTests` and `ToolchainOnThisMachineTests`. The same thread ids in the same frames across samples seven minutes apart, with 3.4 seconds of CPU consumed in twelve minutes of elapsed time. Meanwhile `codesign -v` on the same binary returned instantly from a shell, so the system was not the bottleneck.

WHAT THAT MAKES FRAGILE. With the pool at fourteen of sixteen there are two slots left, and anything that needs a third while holding a lock other tests block on deadlocks the whole run. `TrailIsolation` is exactly such a lock: every trail suite takes it from a cooperative thread. PRO-0083's witnesses hit this three separate ways and each is now avoided in the test rather than in the product — blocking work moved onto owned threads, the trail held only across code that never suspends, and the witness sessions given probes that answer from a table instead of from this machine. Before those, the suite ran to a verdict in 12 to 26 seconds with these files skipped and never returned with them present.

NOT FIXED HERE, and it is a product-shaped question rather than a test one: whether a health report should do a blocking code-signature check on the actor at all, or hand it to a detached executor and report `unconfirmed` until it answers. The same shape is already recorded once as DEF-029, where the wall clock rather than the pool was what moved. Recorded because a suite that deadlocks under load deadlocks in CI, where load is normal.

RE-MEASURED ON THE RESUME, 2026-08-21: still live, and the mechanism narrowed a step further - see DEF-044. The blocked frame is `Security::Dispatch::Group::wait()`, so the cooperative thread is not merely slow inside a syscall, it is waiting on libdispatch global-pool workers that this suite's child processes compete for. The three test-side mitigations recorded above reduce this item's contribution but cannot remove it: the concurrency that saturates the pool is the wiring suites' own.

defect.title: SignatureVerdictCache verifies outside its own lock, so N cold caches verify one file N times at once
defect.found: PRO-0083 resume: the full suite failed deterministically at 143s with two bound overruns, and wedged entirely at higher load
defect.detail:
`SignatureVerdictCache.verdict(for:)` takes its lock, misses, RELEASES the lock, and only then calls `verify(path)`. Concurrent callers with a cold cache therefore all enter `SecStaticCodeCheckValidity` together rather than one doing the work and the rest waiting on it. There is no single-flight, and the doc comment above the method - "verifying only when the file is one this cache has not already seen" - describes behaviour the method does not have under concurrency.

MEASURED 2026-08-21 by `sample`, twice, on two separate full runs: fifteen of the sixteen cooperative threads inside `SecStaticCodeCheckValidityWithErrors` -> `SecStaticCode::staticValidate` -> `Security::Dispatch::Group::wait()` -> `_dispatch_group_wait_slow` -> `__ulock_wait`, in ScreenRecordingProbeWiringTests, ObscuraPresenceWiringTests, ToolchainDoctorTests and GuestProviderTests. `staticValidate` farms its page hashing to the libdispatch global pool and waits on a group, so a blocked cooperative thread is waiting on a worker pool that any second load can starve.

WHY A PER-INSTANCE FIX DOES NOT CLOSE IT: each Session holds its own cache, so the fifteen concurrent verifications are fifteen SEPARATE cache instances each legitimately missing once. Single-flighting one instance would not deduplicate them; the dedupe would have to be process-wide, which is a design change rather than a lock move. Recorded rather than fixed for that reason.

ATTRIBUTION, measured rather than assumed: the full suite WITHOUT this item's two suites passes 1,818 tests in 6.5 seconds with ScreenRecordingProbeWiringTests' bounded test taking 0.655s. This item's two suites alone pass in 9.5 seconds. Together the run takes 143 seconds and that same bounded test overruns its 5-second bound to 10.6s. The suites do not fail each other's assertions; they exhaust a shared pool.

INTERMITTENT AFTER THIS ITEM'S FIX, and measured as such. Removing the forging arm's launch took the full run from 143s to 16.4s and from four issues to one, and it went green at 1,827 tests in 21.376s. It does not go green every time: sampled during a later wedge, fifteen threads sat in the same staticValidate stack and NONE of them were this item's - `pro83.`-named threads in the sample: zero, ExternalWitnessTests frames: zero.
